nodes.description: A negative finding curated as a node because it is load-bearing rather than incidental. This node is the reason the disease is missed.

nodes.description: The liver holds subnormal glycogen. Note the calibration: the classic descriptions say markedly decreased rather than absent, and the original linkage study reported the content as only moderately decreased despite enzyme activity being nil - residual glycogen presumably reflects other minor routes of glucosyl transfer, so "no glycogen at all" would overstate it. The functional point is that the reserve is too small to buffer a fast, and too small to enlarge the organ.

nodes.description: The integrating node, and the diagnostic signature of the disease. Because the liver can neither store glucose when fed nor release it when fasted, glycemia swings across the day between postprandial hyperglycemia with lactic acidemia and fasting ketotic hypoglycemia, instead of being buffered flat. Continuous or serial glucose monitoring shows daily fluctuation between the two poles; neither pole alone is specific, and it is the oscillation that is.

nodes.description: Hepatocytes cannot polymerise incoming glucose into glycogen. Two consequences branch from this one node, and holding both in view is what makes the disease legible: the liver has no glycogen reserve to draw on when fasting, and it has nowhere to put dietary glucose when fed. Everything downstream is one of those two branches.

nodes.description: The fasted half of the disease. Glucose falls, ketones rise, and - this is the discriminating detail - lactate and alanine are LOW rather than high. Low lactate follows from gluconeogenesis running at full tilt and consuming lactate as substrate, and low alanine from its consumption as a gluconeogenic precursor; both are the mirror image of GSD I, where the gluconeogenic block dams lactate up and produces fasting lactic acidosis. Symptoms typically surface in late infancy, when overnight feeds are dropped.

nodes.description: The mainstay, and entirely dietary. Frequent daytime meals high in protein supply gluconeogenic precursors, which works here precisely because gluconeogenesis is intact - the same logic as in GSD VI, and the opposite of GSD I where the gluconeogenic step is itself blocked. Uncooked cornstarch at bedtime, dosed at roughly 1-1.5 g/kg and repeated six-hourly during illness, provides slow-release glucose across the overnight fast. Preventing hyperketonemia is not just symptom relief: it lifts the feedback inhibition of alanine release from muscle, so the diet also protects the gluconeogenic substrate supply it depends on.

meta.association: Biallelic loss-of-function variants in GYS2, which encodes the liver isoform of glycogen synthase, cause GSD 0a. Linkage to the GYS2 locus was established in five families and confirmed by expression of the mutant enzymes, and the allelic spectrum has widened steadily since - from sixteen reported mutations in 2010 to a further seven novel variants in a single 2020 next-generation-sequencing cohort. GYS1, the muscle isoform, causes a separate disease (GSD 0b) and is not involved here.

nodes.description: An amplifying loop that explains why a fast that is tolerated for hours can decompensate abruptly. Severe hyperketonemia and elevated free fatty acids suppress alanine release from skeletal muscle; alanine is the principal gluconeogenic precursor, and gluconeogenesis is the only remaining route to hepatic glucose output. The compensation that keeps this disease mild is therefore self-limiting.

nodes.description: Biallelic GYS2 loss of function removes the liver isoform of glycogen synthase, the enzyme that transfers glucose from UDP-glucose onto the growing alpha-1,4 chain. This is the synthesis-side counterpart of the phosphorylase lesion in GSD VI: the same polymer, the opposite direction of the reaction, and therefore the opposite tissue consequence. Liver enzyme activity in affected children is extremely low or unmeasurable.

nodes.description: In the postabsorptive state the liver has almost no glycogen to mobilise, so hepatic glucose output rests entirely on gluconeogenesis. Both gluconeogenesis and fatty-acid oxidation are intact here - the lesion is confined to the synthetic step - and their preservation is what keeps the hypoglycemia milder than in GSD I while simultaneously making it ketotic.

nodes.description: The other half of the diet, and the half that is specific to this disease rather than shared with the hepatic glycogenoses generally. Because ingested glucose is shunted to lactate, a rapidly absorbed carbohydrate load produces postprandial lactic acidosis; complex low-glycemic-index carbohydrate blunts that. The stated therapeutic goal is explicitly two-sided - prevent the fasting hyperketonemia AND the post-prandial lactic acidosis - which is the diurnal swing restated as a treatment target.

nodes.description: The fed half of the disease, and the part that is most often misread. A substantial fraction of dietary carbohydrate is normally parked in hepatic glycogen; with that sink removed, glucose and other sugars taken up by the liver are diverted into glycolysis. The liver therefore converts a meal into lactate instead of into stored polymer.
